transfer_time: none (answers written directly on the answer sheet within the 60 minutes)
marking: 1 mark per correct answer; raw score out of 40 is converted to a band (whole or half band). Published Academic reference points: about 15/40 = band 5, 23/40 = band 6, 30/40 = band 7, 35/40 = band 8 (exact conversion varies slightly between test versions).
text_sources: Books, journals, magazines, newspapers and online sources written for a non-specialist audience; topics of general interest to undergraduate or postgraduate students. Styles may be narrative, descriptive or discursive/argumentative, and at least one text contains detailed logical argument. Texts may include diagrams, graphs or illustrations. Technical terms come with a simple glossary definition.

passages.paragraphs: 5–9 paragraphs, labelled A, B, C… when a matching-paragraph task is used
passages.difficulty: Most accessible (about CEFR B2). Mainly factual, descriptive or narrative, e.g. the history of an invention, a species or a natural process. Information is mostly explicit and paraphrase is fairly direct.
passages.typical_sources: Popular-science magazines, quality newspapers, general-interest non-fiction and educational websites.

passages.paragraphs: 5–9 paragraphs, labelled A, B, C… when a matching-paragraph task is used
passages.difficulty: Moderate (about CEFR B2–C1). More discursive: describes research, a development or a problem with several viewpoints, named researchers and findings. Paraphrase between the questions and the text is less direct.
passages.typical_sources: Science and social-science journalism, reports of research studies, magazine features on technology, business, psychology or the environment.

passages.paragraphs: 5–9 paragraphs, labelled A, B, C… when a matching-paragraph task is used
passages.difficulty: Hardest (about CEFR C1–C2). Argumentative or discursive, with detailed logical argument and the writer's own views and claims. Abstract vocabulary, complex syntax, hedging, and implicit relationships between ideas.
passages.typical_sources: Academic-style essays and opinion pieces for educated general readers, book extracts and review articles (history of ideas, philosophy of science, linguistics, economics, the arts).

passage_design_rules: Each passage carries 2–3 question types (at least two), grouped in consecutive blocks; each block has its own rubric with the question range.
Question numbers run 1–40 across the test; each passage's questions continue from the previous passage.

The paper-based booklet says 'You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.' (and similarly 'Questions 14–26 … Reading Passage 2', 'Questions 27–40 … Reading Passage 3'). Passages have a title and sometimes a subtitle.
MATCHING_HEADINGS questions are printed BEFORE the passage; all other question blocks follow it.
The last question of Passage 3 is often a global question, e.g. 'Which of the following is the most suitable title for Reading Passage 3?' (MULTIPLE_CHOICE A–D).
Never test the same sentence of the passage twice across different question blocks.
delivery_notes: Rubric templates below are the paper-based wording. In computer-delivered IELTS the 'Write … in boxes … on your answer sheet' line is replaced by on-screen answer entry (typing, clicking or drag-and-drop), and the rest of the rubric is unchanged.
Candidates may read the questions and passages in any order; no extra time is given at the end.

rubric_placeholders.{from}: first question number of the block, e.g. 1
rubric_placeholders.{to}: last question number of the block, e.g. 7
rubric_placeholders.{word_limit}: an item from word_limit_phrases, e.g. 'NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS'
rubric_placeholders.{last_letter}: last option letter, e.g. G for options A–G
rubric_placeholders.{last_numeral}: last heading numeral in lower-case Roman numerals, e.g. viii
rubric_placeholders.{count_word}: number written as a word, e.g. 'seven' (paragraphs), 'TWO' / 'THREE' (letters to choose, in capitals)
rubric_placeholders.{paragraph_list}: paragraphs to be matched when one is given as an example, e.g. 'A and C–G'
rubric_placeholders.{features}: plural name of the option set in MATCHING_FEATURES, e.g. 'researchers', 'countries', 'periods of time'
rubric_placeholders.{list_title}: title of the option box, e.g. 'List of Researchers'

word_limit_phrases: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER
NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER
answer_sheet_conventions: Answers are written directly on the answer sheet (in pencil) during the 60 minutes; there is no transfer time. Unanswered questions score 0 and wrong answers lose nothing, so every question should be attempted.
Spelling must be correct. For 'from the passage' answers, copy the words exactly as spelt in the passage; a misspelt answer is wrong.
Answers may be written in upper or lower case (writing everything in capitals is acceptable).
Exceeding the word limit makes the answer wrong even if it contains the right words. 'NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER' allows, e.g., 'two words', 'a number', or 'two words and a number'.
Hyphenated words (e.g. 'check-in', 'well-known') count as one word. Contracted forms (e.g. 'they're') are not tested.
Numbers may be written as figures (1, 2, 1990) or words (one, two). A number counts as a number, not as a word, under 'AND/OR A NUMBER' limits.
Completion answers must be words taken from the passage, unchanged in form (no changing a noun to a verb or singular to plural); the gap is designed so that the passage form fits grammatically.

Articles and other words the key shows in brackets are optional: '(the) harbour' accepts 'harbour' and 'the harbour' (if within the word limit). Alternative correct answers are separated by a slash in the key.

TRUE / FALSE / NOT GIVEN and YES / NO / NOT GIVEN answers must use the set required by the rubric: writing TRUE for a YES/NO question (or YES for a TRUE/FALSE question) is marked wrong. In this app, require the full words; abbreviations such as T, F, NG are not accepted.
Letter answers: write only the letter (A, B, C…); for headings, only the lower-case Roman numeral (i, ii, iii…). Writing two answers for one question scores 0.
MULTIPLE_CHOICE_MULTI ('Choose TWO letters'): each question number carries one mark and the letters may be given in either order.
Word-bank tasks (summary 'using the list of words, A–…'): write the letter, not the word.

MULTIPLE_CHOICE.what_it_tests: Detailed understanding of specific points, or general understanding of the main points, the writer's purpose or the text as a whole.
design_rules: Four options A–D (Academic Reading always uses four); the stem is a question or an incomplete sentence completed by the options.

Exactly one option is fully supported by the text; each distractor is plausible: mentioned in the text but not answering the question, true only in part, contradicted by the text, or a common-sense assumption the text doesn't support.
Paraphrase the stem and the correct option; don't reuse the key sentence's distinctive words in the correct option only (word-matching must not give the answer away).
Options are of similar length and grammatical form; avoid 'all of the above' and 'none of the above'.
Questions follow the order of information in the passage; a global question (main purpose / best title) may come last and covers the whole passage.
Usually 3–6 questions per block.

MULTIPLE_CHOICE_MULTI.answer_format: One distinct letter per question number; together the letters form the set of correct options, accepted in any order.
MULTIPLE_CHOICE_MULTI.what_it_tests: Locating and understanding several specific points, e.g. which advantages, reasons or findings the writer mentions.
design_rules: The stem follows the rubric and asks for the set explicitly, e.g. 'Which TWO … are mentioned by the writer?' / 'Which THREE of the following …?'.
Use 5 options (A–E) for TWO answers; 6–7 options (A–F/G) are also used; use 6–7 options for THREE answers.
The block sits in sequence with neighbouring questions, but the correct options may come from anywhere in the relevant section and in any order.
Distractors are things the text mentions in a different role (e.g. a disadvantage when advantages are asked for), claims attributed to someone else, or ideas not stated.
Each question number is worth one mark, so a TWO-letter block uses two consecutive question numbers.

TRUE_FALSE_NOT_GIVEN.rubric_template:
Questions {from}–{to}
Do the following statements agree with the information given in {passage}?
In boxes {from}–{to} on your answer sheet, write
TRUE if the statement agrees with the information
FALSE if the statement contradicts the information
NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this
TRUE_FALSE_NOT_GIVEN.what_it_tests: Recognising specific factual information in the text and telling contradiction (FALSE) apart from absence of information (NOT GIVEN), without using outside knowledge.
design_rules: Typically 4–8 statements per block; use each of TRUE, FALSE and NOT GIVEN at least once and avoid long runs of the same answer.
Statements are factual, not about the writer's opinion (that is YES_NO_NOT_GIVEN), and follow passage order.
TRUE: a paraphrase of one specific sentence or clause; don't copy wording.

FALSE: must directly contradict something the text states (e.g. a changed quantity, time, cause, comparative, sequence, or an absolute word such as 'always'/'only'/'first' the text contradicts). Being merely unsupported is NOT GIVEN, not FALSE.

NOT GIVEN: clearly on the passage's topic and next to a real sentence (share its subject), but the text neither confirms nor denies the specific claim (e.g. adds an unstated reason, a comparison or superlative the text never makes, or a detail about the future). General knowledge must not settle it.
Each statement tests one idea. Avoid double negatives and statements that are true or false only because of trivial wording.
Statements are paraphrased; don't put the passage's distinctive words only into the TRUE statements.

YES_NO_NOT_GIVEN.rubric_template:
Questions {from}–{to}
Do the following statements agree with the {views_or_claims} of the writer in {passage}?
In boxes {from}–{to} on your answer sheet, write
YES if the statement agrees with the {views_or_claims} of the writer
NO if the statement contradicts the {views_or_claims} of the writer
NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this
YES_NO_NOT_GIVEN.what_it_tests: Recognising the writer's opinions, attitudes or claims (including implied stance) and telling contradiction apart from absence of a view.
design_rules: Only use with passages where the writer takes positions (argumentative or discursive texts, typically Passage 3). 'views' suits opinion/evaluation; 'claims' suits assertions of fact the writer makes.
Typically 4–7 statements; use each answer at least once; statements follow passage order.
YES/NO depend on the WRITER's stance, not on views the writer reports from other people (a researcher's view the writer disputes → NO if the statement matches the researcher).
NOT GIVEN: the topic is mentioned but the writer expresses no view on this specific point.
Look for evaluative language in the text (admittedly, it is doubtful whether, rightly, the real problem is) to anchor YES/NO statements.

MATCHING_INFORMATION.rubric_template:
Questions {from}–{to}
{passage} has {count_word} paragraphs, A–{last_letter}.
Which paragraph contains the following information?
Write the correct letter, A–{last_letter}, in boxes {from}–{to} on your answer sheet.
NB You may use any letter more than once.
rubric_variants:
Questions {from}–{to}
{passage} has {count_word} sections, A–{last_letter}.
Which section contains the following information?
Write the correct letter, A–{last_letter}, in boxes {from}–{to} on your answer sheet.
MATCHING_INFORMATION.what_it_tests: Scanning for specific information (a detail, example, reason, description, comparison, summary or explanation) rather than main ideas.
design_rules: Paragraphs must be labelled A, B, C… in the passage.
Each item names a TYPE of information plus its content, e.g. 'a reference to…', 'an example of…', 'an explanation of why…', 'a comparison between…', 'a description of…', 'a prediction about…'.
Items are NOT in passage order; not every paragraph needs to be used.
Add 'NB You may use any letter more than once.' only when at least one paragraph is the answer to two items; omit the NB line otherwise.
Each item must be locatable in exactly one paragraph; paraphrase so that searching for keywords alone does not work.
Usually 4–7 items.

MATCHING_HEADINGS.rubric_template:
Questions {from}–{to}
{passage} has {count_word} paragraphs, A–{last_letter}.
Choose the correct heading for each paragraph from the list of headings below.
Write the correct number, i–{last_numeral}, in boxes {from}–{to} on your answer sheet.

List of Headings
rubric_variants:
Questions {from}–{to}
{passage} has {count_word} paragraphs, A–{last_letter}.
Choose the correct heading for paragraphs {paragraph_list} from the list of headings below.
Write the correct number, i–{last_numeral}, in boxes {from}–{to} on your answer sheet.

List of Headings

Questions {from}–{to}
{passage} has {count_word} sections, A–{last_letter}.
Choose the correct heading for each section from the list of headings below.
Write the correct number, i–{last_numeral}, in boxes {from}–{to} on your answer sheet.

List of Headings
MATCHING_HEADINGS.answer_format: One lower-case Roman numeral per question (i, ii, iii…).
MATCHING_HEADINGS.what_it_tests: Identifying the main idea or general topic of a paragraph or section and telling it apart from supporting detail.
design_rules: Always more headings than paragraphs to be matched (usually 2–3 extra); headings are numbered with lower-case Roman numerals.
Each heading can be used only once; some headings are never used. Some paragraphs may be left out of the task.
One paragraph may be matched already as an example ('Example: Paragraph A — iii'); then use the {paragraph_list} rubric variant and don't use that heading again.
Question stems are just 'Paragraph B', 'Paragraph C'… in passage order; the task is printed before the passage.
A correct heading summarises the WHOLE paragraph's main idea in paraphrase; distractor headings match a single detail, a keyword or a nearby paragraph's idea.
Headings are short noun phrases or clauses (about 4–10 words) with no end punctuation.

MATCHING_FEATURES.what_it_tests: Recognising relationships and connections between facts, and which person, period, place or theory a statement, finding or opinion belongs to; skimming and scanning, then close reading.
design_rules: The options (A–E typical; up to about A–J) are features named in the text, such as researchers, organisations, countries, periods, products or theories. List them in the order they first appear in the text.
Statements are paraphrased findings, claims or descriptions, NOT in passage order.
Some options may be unused and some used more than once; include the NB line only if an option is used more than once.
Where a person is mentioned in several places, make sure only one option can match each statement.
Usually 4–7 statements.

MATCHING_SENTENCE_ENDINGS.what_it_tests: Understanding main ideas and how parts of a sentence-level proposition fit together (cause and effect, conditions, findings).
design_rules: More endings than beginnings (usually 2–3 extra); each ending is used at most once.
Sentence beginnings follow passage order; endings are listed in random order.
Every ending must fit grammatically with every beginning, so that grammar alone can't show the answer.
Distractor endings reuse passage vocabulary but combine ideas the text does not connect.
Usually 3–6 beginnings.

SENTENCE_COMPLETION.rubric_template:
Questions {from}–{to}
Complete the sentences below.
Choose {word_limit} from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in boxes {from}–{to} on your answer sheet.
SENTENCE_COMPLETION.answer_format: Word(s) and/or a number copied exactly from the passage, within the word limit.
SENTENCE_COMPLETION.what_it_tests: Finding detail or specific information and checking that it completes the sentence's meaning and grammar.
design_rules: One gap per sentence; the sentence paraphrases a passage sentence, and the gap is the key content word(s).
The answer appears verbatim in the passage and fits the gap grammatically without any change of form.
No answer word may appear elsewhere in its own stem; only one passage phrase can correctly fill the gap.
Prefer ONE WORD ONLY or NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS; state any number allowance in the word limit.
Usually 3–6 sentences.

SUMMARY_COMPLETION.rubric_template:
Questions {from}–{to}
Complete the summary below.
Choose {word_limit} from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in boxes {from}–{to} on your answer sheet.
SUMMARY_COMPLETION.answer_format: Words from the passage within the word limit, or (word-bank variant) one letter per gap.
SUMMARY_COMPLETION.what_it_tests: Understanding details and/or main ideas of one part of the text, including which word class each gap needs.
design_rules: Summarise one section of the passage (not normally the whole text); give the summary a short title.
Gaps are usually in the order of that section, but order is not guaranteed; all answers come from the same part of the text.
Words-from-passage variant: answers appear verbatim and fit grammatically; one correct phrase per gap.

Word-bank variant: more options than gaps (typically 3–6 extra); options are often synonyms rather than the passage's own words; several options should fit each gap grammatically, and distractors share the gaps' word classes.
Usually 4–7 gaps.

NOTE_COMPLETION.rubric_template:
Questions {from}–{to}
Complete the notes below.
Choose {word_limit} from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in boxes {from}–{to} on your answer sheet.
NOTE_COMPLETION.answer_format: Words and/or numbers from the passage within the word limit.
NOTE_COMPLETION.what_it_tests: Understanding details and how points relate to each other, presented in condensed note form.
design_rules: Notes have a title, sub-headings and bullet/dash lines written in note style (articles and verbs often dropped).
Answers come from one part of the text; they usually follow its order, but this is not guaranteed.
Each gap is a key fact (a noun or noun phrase is most common); answers verbatim from the passage.
Usually 4–8 gaps.

TABLE_COMPLETION.rubric_template:
Questions {from}–{to}
Complete the table below.
Choose {word_limit} from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in boxes {from}–{to} on your answer sheet.
TABLE_COMPLETION.answer_format: Words and/or numbers from the passage within the word limit.
TABLE_COMPLETION.what_it_tests: Understanding details and classifying information into clear categories (e.g. period / development / effect).
design_rules: Use a table only when the text naturally supplies parallel information across categories (columns) for several items (rows).
Cells are in note style; gaps are spread across rows and columns and numbered left-to-right, top-to-bottom.
Answers come from one part of the text and may not follow text order.
Usually 3–6 gaps.

FLOW_CHART_COMPLETION.rubric_template:
Questions {from}–{to}
Complete the flow-chart below.
Choose {word_limit} from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in boxes {from}–{to} on your answer sheet.
FLOW_CHART_COMPLETION.answer_format: Words and/or numbers from the passage within the word limit.
FLOW_CHART_COMPLETION.what_it_tests: Following a process, procedure or chain of events described in the text and understanding the sequence.
design_rules: Only for passages that describe a sequence (a manufacturing process, experiment method, historical chain of events, life cycle).
Boxes/steps are linked by arrows in the true order of the process, which the text may present out of order.
Each step is a short note-style clause; gaps are key nouns or verbs.
Usually 3–6 gaps.

DIAGRAM_LABEL_COMPLETION.rubric_template:
Questions {from}–{to}
Label the diagram below.
Choose {word_limit} from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in boxes {from}–{to} on your answer sheet.
DIAGRAM_LABEL_COMPLETION.answer_format: Words and/or numbers from the passage within the word limit.
DIAGRAM_LABEL_COMPLETION.what_it_tests: Understanding a detailed description in the text (a device, structure, building or natural feature) and relating it to a diagram.
design_rules: The passage must describe the physical parts, positions and functions clearly enough for the labels to be found (e.g. 'a chamber beneath the…', 'a pipe connects…').
Some labels are given to orient the reader; the gaps label parts named in the text.
Answers come from one part of the text and may not follow text order.
Usually 3–6 labels.

SHORT_ANSWER.rubric_template:
Questions {from}–{to}
Answer the questions below.
Choose {word_limit} from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in boxes {from}–{to} on your answer sheet.
SHORT_ANSWER.answer_format: Words and/or numbers from the passage within the word limit.
SHORT_ANSWER.what_it_tests: Finding and understanding specific factual details (who, what, which, where, when, how many).
design_rules: Wh-questions that paraphrase the passage; each has one short factual answer.
Answers are verbatim from the passage; numbers may be written as figures or words.
Questions follow passage order.
Usually 3–6 questions; NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER is the common limit.
